concepts.concept: Comparable and Comparator for custom ordering

futureAppearances.label: BinaryHeaps
futureAppearances.description: BinaryHeap is generic over Comparable so that heapifyUp and heapifyDown can compare elements without knowing their type—the same contract established when implementing Comparable on Shape subclasses.

futureAppearances.label: GraphSurfing — Dijkstra's algorithm
futureAppearances.description: Dijkstra's priority queue entries are ordered by tentative distance; understanding how to express a total ordering via Comparable (or a Comparator passed to PriorityQueue) is required to implement the min-priority queue that drives the algorithm.

futureAppearances.label: EditorTrees
futureAppearances.description: Though EditorTrees nodes are ordered by rank rather than a Comparable key, the invariant that defines 'correct position' parallels the Comparable contract: a consistent, transitive total order must be maintained across every add and delete.

futureAppearances.label: Exam 2 / Final
futureAppearances.description: Exam problems on sorting and tree operations often require writing or tracing a Comparator to verify that students can express custom orderings independently of the Comparable default.

futureAppearances.label: BST assignment
futureAppearances.description: A sorted linked list maintains O(n) insert with sorted order; the BST assignment replaces that with O(log n) average insert while preserving sorted in-order traversal—making the sorted linked list the direct motivating predecessor.

futureAppearances.label: EditorTrees
futureAppearances.description: AVL trees (EditorTrees) extend the BST's sorted structure with guaranteed O(log n) worst-case cost; the progression from sorted linked list → BST → AVL tree is the central narrative of the course's first half.

futureAppearances.label: BinaryHeaps
futureAppearances.description: A min-heap also enforces a structural ordering, but only the partial order property (parent ≤ children) rather than full sorted order—understanding why full sorted order costs more motivates the heap's design.

futureAppearances.label: GraphSurfing
futureAppearances.description: Java's TreeSet (a Red-Black BST) is used in graph algorithms to maintain vertex sets in sorted order with O(log n) operations; experience with sorted structure invariants from this assignment directly applies.

futureAppearances.label: BinaryHeaps assignment
futureAppearances.description: BinaryHeaps implements the same three core operations—insert, findMin, removeMin—but achieves O(log n) cost via the heap property and array-based storage instead of a linear scan.

futureAppearances.label: GraphSurfing — Dijkstra's algorithm
futureAppearances.description: Dijkstra's algorithm is driven entirely by removeMin: at each step the unvisited vertex with smallest tentative distance is extracted from the priority queue. Understanding that removeMin is the bottleneck operation directly informs the O((V + E) log V) cost analysis.

futureAppearances.label: HW on heaps
futureAppearances.description: Homework problems ask students to trace heapifyDown after removeMin on a given heap array, requiring exact understanding of the operation semantics implemented here.

futureAppearances.label: BST assignment
futureAppearances.description: BST contains() is binary search on a pointer-linked structure: each comparison eliminates half the remaining search space exactly as array binary search does, making testBinarySearchEfficiency the motivating complexity argument for BSTs.

futureAppearances.label: EditorTrees get(int pos)
futureAppearances.description: get(int pos) navigates by rank in O(log n)—a generalization of binary search where the 'midpoint' is the current node's left-subtree size rather than a computed array index.

futureAppearances.label: Exam questions on complexity
futureAppearances.description: Exam and homework problems on O(log n) algorithms (BST search, heap operations, merge sort) trace back to binary search as the prototype; students who understand why binary search is O(log n) can extend that argument to tree height and heap depth.

futureAppearances.label: GraphSurfing
futureAppearances.description: Binary search over edge weights or sorted adjacency data appears in some graph problem variants; more broadly, the O(log n) search paradigm underlies the efficient priority queue that powers Dijkstra's algorithm.

concepts.concept: GCD via Euclid's algorithm and runtime analysis

futureAppearances.label: Algorithm analysis / HW
futureAppearances.description: The worst-case input for Euclid's algorithm (consecutive Fibonacci numbers) is a standard homework problem in CSSE 230 that requires the same recurrence reasoning used in the AVL tree minimum-node proof—both rely on Fibonacci growth to establish a logarithmic bound.

futureAppearances.label: EditorTrees height proofs
futureAppearances.description: Proving that an AVL tree of height H has at least S(H) = S(H-1) + S(H-2) + 1 nodes uses Fibonacci recurrences, the same mathematical structure that governs Euclid worst-case analysis.

futureAppearances.label: Exam 1
futureAppearances.description: Exam 1 typically includes a worst-case runtime question on a recursive algorithm; Euclid's algorithm is the template for reasoning about how remaindering shrinks problem size, a technique students apply to merge sort and BST height analysis.

concepts.concept: N-gram frequency counting and string processing

futureAppearances.label: GraphSurfing
futureAppearances.description: Graph problems often involve accumulating edge or vertex labels as strings; the pattern of iterating a sequence and updating a frequency map (HashMap or TreeMap) used in n-gram counting reappears when building adjacency lists or computing degree histograms.

futureAppearances.label: BST / TreeMap use
futureAppearances.description: N-gram counting with a TreeMap is a direct application of BST-ordered map operations; the assignment motivates why BST-backed maps deliver O(log n) put/get while HashMap delivers O(1) average—a trade-off students revisit in every subsequent data-structure choice.

concepts.concept: Anagram detection and character frequency analysis

futureAppearances.label: Hashing / HashMap (lecture and HW)
futureAppearances.description: The canonical O(n) anagram algorithm uses a frequency array or HashMap; once hashing is introduced, students are asked to re-examine why anagram detection is O(n) with a hash map but O(n log n) with a sorted structure, reinforcing the cost model.

futureAppearances.label: Exam problems on maps and sets
futureAppearances.description: Exam problems that ask students to choose between HashMap, TreeMap, and sorted arrays for membership queries are direct descendants of the anagram problem, where the right data structure determines algorithmic efficiency.
